module_title: Launch Vehicles and Major Historic Missions
introduction: To put satellites into space, you need rockets (Launch Vehicles). ISRO has developed a highly reliable fleet of rockets, leading to some of the most historic planetary missions in the 21st century.

core_concepts.title: PSLV: The Workhorse of ISRO
core_concepts.description: PSLV (Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle) is ISRO's most reliable rocket. It mainly places Earth Observation satellites into **Sun-Synchronous Polar Orbits** (LEO). It has a 4-stage engine (Solid-Liquid-Solid-Liquid). It was used for Chandrayaan-1 and Mangalyaan.

core_concepts.title: GSLV / LVM3: The Heavy Lifter
core_concepts.description: GSLV (Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle), specifically the LVM3 (Launch Vehicle Mark 3), is designed to carry heavy communication satellites into GEO. It uses a highly complex **Cryogenic Engine** in its final stage (using liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen at extremely low temperatures).

core_concepts.title: Mangalyaan (Mars Orbiter Mission - MOM)
core_concepts.description: Launched in 2013 via PSLV. It made India the **first Asian nation** to reach Martian orbit and the **first nation in the world** to do so on its maiden (first) attempt. It cost merely $74 million (cheaper than the movie *Gravity*).

core_concepts.title: NavIC (India's Own GPS)
core_concepts.description: NavIC (Navigation with Indian Constellation) is India's regional satellite navigation system. It consists of a constellation of **7 satellites** providing accurate real-time positioning and timing services over India and a region extending 1,500 km around it.

important_entities.name: Chandrayaan-1 (2008)
important_entities.significance: India's first lunar mission carried an instrument called the Moon Mineralogy Mapper (M3), provided by NASA, which conclusively discovered the presence of water molecules on the lunar surface.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation:
The Biggest Exam Trap: 
- **Geosynchronous Orbit:** Takes 24 hours to orbit, but can be tilted (inclined) relative to the equator. It appears to move in a figure-8 shape in the sky. 
- **Geostationary Orbit:** Takes 24 hours AND is exactly above the equator with zero inclination. It stays fixed at one exact point in the sky. 
*(All Geostationary orbits are Geosynchronous, but not vice-versa).*

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: P for Pole, G for Geo
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: PSLV generally launches into Polar orbits (going North-South around the Earth). GSLV launches into Geosynchronous orbits (going East-West along the equator).

exam_strategy_tips: A highly repeated State PCS/UPSC question: 'What is the full form of NavIC's original project name?' Answer: IRNSS (Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System).
